newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda refugees spend night on Zaire border.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda refugees spend night on Zaire border.

text.p: Huddled under plastic sheeting with their belongings, hundreds of thousands of returning Rwandan Hutu refugees spent a cold night in the open around a Zaire border post.

As night fell on Saturday, the Zairean frontier town of Goma filled with the haze of smoke from fires as thousands of refugee families cooked a final evening meal in Zaire before preparing to rejoin at daybreak the long, snaking column entering Rwanda.
A total of 200,000 Rwandan Hutus among the more than one million who fled to Zaire in 1994 had so far returned since Friday, the U.N. refugee agency said on Saturday.
"We are overwhelmed," said Ray Wilkinson, spokesman of the United Nations UNHCR refugee agency.
"To use that overused phrase, this is of biblical proportions. I don't think we could plan in taking 700,000 people in a few days -- the crisis right now is to get them back home," he added.

The refugees are running out of food and clean water. There is no sanitation. The crush is relentless. Conditions provide a perfect breeding ground for such diseases as cholera which killed tens of thousands of Hutus in Zaire two years ago.

Aid agencies have supplies of food nearby but lack the means amid the chaos to distribute it. Aid workers gave up trying to register the refugees and hope they will return quickly to their villages and replant their fields.

The mass exodus began suddenly on Friday when an alliance of Zairean rebels forced Hutu militiamen, who had been preventing the refugees from leaving, to flee the teeming camps they had ruthlessly controlled since 1994.

The militia and former Hutu government troops had spearheaded the genocide of some one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994, before being driven out by Tutsi rebels who went on to establish a new government in the capital Kigali.

The UNHCR said its officials met Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila and he "suggested" that Rwanda refugees from other areas such as Bukavu further south could begin moving back into Rwanda from Tuesday.

In Washington, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the rapidly changing situation could force a change in plans in the Canadian-led multinational force the U.N. Security Council approved by unanimous vote on Friday.
Perry told a news conference the United States would consult with its allies after receiving a report this weekend from a survey team in the area.
But Rwanda said the refugee exodus meant the force was obsolete before it was even deployed and the world should send aid instead to help Rwanda settle the newcomers.

"Our position is that the force was coming to create this corridor for the refugees to come home and now they are coming home. So we don't see any need for the force to come," said Joseph Bideri, spokesman for President Pasteur Bizimungu.
U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien, in Kigali on a whistle-stop regional tour, was yet to see Bizimungu or powerful vice-president and defence minister Paul Kagame, a government official said.
Fighting continued on Saturday between the Zairean rebels, who have been supported by the Tutsi-dominated army in Rwanda, and the Hutu forces which have fought alongside Zairean government troops.
The eastern rebellion could yet threaten the stability of the Zairean government far away in Kinshasa whose president, Mobutu Sese Seko, has been absent for months in Europe.
Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo said in France on Saturday that Mobutu would soon return home to oversee the refugee aid mission following his treatment for cancer in Switzerland.
